newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian gay minister a seeming exception in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Belgian gay minister a seeming exception in Europe.

text.p: A court probe into allegations that Belgian Deputy Prime Minister Elio Di Rupo had sex with under-age boys has led to his exposure as a homosexual and opened up debate on what had been largely a taboo issue in European political circles.
In the Netherlands and Denmark, renowned for their libertarian views, the sexual orientation of a government minister is deemed irrelevant.
But in other parts of Europe there is almost a conspiracy of silence, with the latent threat that public exposure of homosexuality could end a political career.

Belgium has been no exception. Di Rupo was known by politicians and journalists to be gay, but his "coming out" has led to calls from some quarters for his resignation regardless of whether the accusations of under-age sex are proved.
Charles Ferdinand Nothomb, chairman of the Christian Democrat government party PSC, said a minister could not be openly gay, a point of view backed by several Roman Catholic newspapers.
"Politicians should not represent sexual deviations but a majority of citizens who adhere to morality," La Libre Belgique said.
Ghent University sociology professor John Vincke rejected this argument.
"We are moving towards an open society in which all minorities are represented. In fact it is important that these minorities have positive role models," he told Reuters.
But with the exception of two publicly identified lesbian ministers in two north European countries, openly homosexual government ministers are a virtual unknown in Europe.
Media pay virtually no media attention to the issue of gays in public office in Germany, a country where the private life of public figures is treated as just that.
Volcker Beck, a parliament member for the environmentalist Greens Party, is one of the rare openly gay politicians.
In Germany, France and in Britain there are periodic rumours about closet homosexuality of ministers, but they mainly remain rumours.
The Netherlands is one of the few European countries where most homosexuals in public life make no secret of their sexual orientation and do not face disapproval from voters.
"Homosexuality among politicians is not contentious," Henk Krol, editor of Gay Krant, told Reuters.
The only openly homosexual minister in recent years was the late Ien Dales, former home affairs minister. She did not deny her homosexuality but declined to discuss it in public.
In Denmark, a recent book named Health Minister Yvonne Herloev Andersen as lesbian.
Andersen did not deny it and reactions to the book focused on its allegation that gay health officials spent too much public money on AIDS care rather than on Andersen's personal sexual preference.
In strongly Catholic European countries like Italy, Spain and Ireland, there are virtualy no known gays in public posts, let alone in government.
Franco Ferrarotti, sociology professor at Rome's La Sapienza University, said that although there have been rumours that some Italian politicians were gay, they were "still in the closet".
"Italy is a heterosexual society which tends to cover up homosexuality. It's okay among artists because they are considered apart from the common people," he said.
